newsitem.title: CHINA: Illegal children migrants fight HK deportation law.
newsitem.headline: Illegal children migrants fight HK deportation law.

text.p: The Hong Kong government on Friday faced an avalanche of court challenges by illegal child immigrants from mainland China who face deportation.
The legal challenges came as the territory's new leader Tung Chee-hwa attended the last session of the China-appointed Preparatory Committee in Beijing.
Tung was also accused of giving media from mainland China preferential treatment, compounding the government's headaches less than two weeks after Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule.

More than 130 mainland-born children have applied for legal aid to mount court challenges against government plans to repatriate them since the territory passed a law on Wednesday to return them to China, even if they have right of abode here.
The assistant director of Legal Aid, Mak Fai-man, said six applications had been approved so far.
The successful applicants plan to launch lawsuits aimed at proving the government's deportation law is unconstitutional.
The tangle involves thousands of children who have been smuggled into Hong Kong, dodging long queues for formal immigration clearance, to join parents already here.
Hong Kong fears a flood of children unless it sends the illegal ones back to China to apply for legal entry.
Smuggled children with a Hong Kong parent have residency rights under the post-colonial constitution, the Basic Law, effective from July 1.

It is estimated that 66,000 children of "separated families" are waiting in China to join parents in Hong Kong, a process that can take years. They often face demands for bribes by Chinese officials who process their papers.
Social activists and legal experts in Hong Kong have condemned the new law as unconstitutional because it retrospectively restricts rights conferred by the Basic Law.

Tung was also criticised by the Hong Kong Journalist Association of excluding local media from covering his first meeting with China's garrison commander last week, while mainland television crews had complete access.
Tung's office denied the accusations. "We are not giving preferential treatment to anybody. We did not deliberately exclude anyone," a Tung spokesman told Reuters on Friday.
In Beijing, the 150-strong Preparatory Committee, in charge of setting up Hong Kong's post-colonial political structure, held its last meeting.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin thanked the caucus, comprised of Hong Kong notables and mainland officials. They chose the 400-member Selection Committee which picked Tung and members of the controversial Provisional Legislature.

Tung told the group that a new era has begun. "This is the last session of the Preparatory Committee. But I feel this is not an end but a new beginning. For history has chosen us and we have made history," he said.
China's top official on Hong Kong affairs, Lu Ping, told reporters in Beijing he was retiring. "My task is completed," he said.
Lu declined to comment on reports that Liao Hui, head of the Overseas Chinese Affairs Office under China's State Council, would replace him next week.
